sections.instruction: Read the narrative text below about a reserve player who is finally sent on in an inter-school final, and answer the questions that follow. Section B, Part 1 [15 marks]. Answer in your own words as far as possible.
sections.passage:
Paragraph 1
I had been in the squad for two years and on the pitch for eleven minutes. The eleven minutes were spread across four matches, all of them already decided, and I knew exactly what they were: politeness.

Paragraph 2
Our coach was not unkind about it. In February he told me plainly that I was the seventh-best midfielder at the school and that there were six shirts. I appreciated the arithmetic. It was easier to carry than encouragement would have been.

Paragraph 3
So I trained. Not out of hope, exactly. It had simply become the shape of my week, and I had stopped asking what it was for.

Paragraph 4
In the final, with nineteen minutes left and the score level, Kai Wen came down badly and did not get up. The coach looked along the bench. There was a pause that I felt in my teeth. Then he said my name.

Paragraph 5
My legs, which had run eight kilometres a day for two years, felt as though they belonged to somebody who had never played football. The first ball that came to me I gave straight back to the other team. The second I did not reach. A parent behind the goal said something I could hear clearly.

Paragraph 6
Then, in the seventy-eighth minute, a ball came loose near the halfway line, and I found that I was already moving. I had watched this team for two years from a plastic chair. I knew, without deciding to know, that their left back always stepped in and never covered behind. I put the ball into the space he had left and Marcus ran onto it and scored.

Paragraph 7
I did not touch the ball again. We won 2-1.

Paragraph 8
Afterwards there were photographs, and in the photographs I am at the edge, half turned away, because I did not yet feel entitled to the middle. The report in the school newsletter mentioned Marcus's finish and did not mention the pass. I read it twice to be sure.

Paragraph 9
My father asked me that night whether I was disappointed. I said no, and then sat with the question a while longer, and found that I had told the truth. Two years of watching from a chair had bought me four seconds of knowing exactly where to put the ball. Nobody in the stand could see that, and it did not stop being true.

questions.stem: Q1. From Paragraph 1, what does the narrator mean by describing his eleven minutes as 'politeness'? [1]
questions.answer: he was only sent on in matches already decided, as a courtesy rather than because he was needed

questions.stem: Q2. Using your own words, explain why the narrator was grateful for the coach's blunt remark in February. (Paragraph 2) [2]
questions.answer: ① the plain arithmetic told him exactly where he stood, leaving no false hope to manage; ② vague encouragement would have been harder to bear because he would have had to keep wondering

questions.stem: Q3. What does the narrator reveal about his motivation in Paragraph 3? [1]
questions.answer: he trained out of habit and routine rather than any expectation of playing

questions.stem: Q4. What is the effect of the description of a pause the narrator 'felt in my teeth' (Paragraph 4)? [2]
questions.answer: it turns a brief silence into a physical sensation, conveying how unbearably tense and drawn-out the moment was for him even though it lasted only seconds

questions.stem: Q5. Using your own words, explain the contrast the narrator draws in Paragraph 5 between his training and his legs. [2]
questions.answer: ① he had prepared physically for two years without missing a day; ② none of that preparation helped in the moment, because nerves made his own body feel unfamiliar and useless

questions.stem: Q6. Why does the writer include the detail of the parent behind the goal? (Paragraph 5) [1]
questions.answer: it shows that his early mistakes were public and openly criticised, deepening his humiliation

questions.stem: Q7. Using your own words, explain how the narrator's two years on the bench helped him make the pass. (Paragraph 6) [2]
questions.answer: ① watching every match had taught him the opposing left back's habit of stepping in without covering; ② this knowledge had become instinctive, so he moved into the gap before he had time to think

questions.stem: Q8. What is the effect of the two very short sentences in Paragraph 7? [2]
questions.answer: the flatness deliberately refuses any triumph — his single decisive contribution is stated as plainly as the score, which suits a narrator who does not claim credit for himself

questions.stem: Q9. From Paragraph 8, give TWO details showing that the narrator's contribution went unrecognised. [1]
questions.answer: he stood at the edge of the photographs, and the newsletter report named only Marcus's goal

questions.stem: Q10. Using your own words, explain what the narrator concludes in the final paragraph. [1]
questions.answer: the worth of his long preparation is real whether or not anyone else notices or records it

sections.instruction: Q11. [4 marks in total] The narrator's dominant feeling changes across the final. For each part of the passage below, choose the ONE word from the bank that best describes how he feels at that moment. Each word may be used once only.
sections.passage: Refer to the same 'The Substitute' narrative in Exercise 1 above. Read the paragraphs named in each question, then choose the single word from the bank that best describes how the narrator feels at that moment.
